psyllium-husk.text: Users take psyllium fibre to feel fuller between meals, so it is easier to hold a calorie deficit and lean out for a more defined face and body. It is well studied for digestion and cholesterol, and trials on weight loss report small effects.

apple-cider-vinegar.text: Apple cider vinegar is drunk diluted for fat loss and used as a skin toner and hair rinse for clearer skin and shinier hair. Small trials exist on weight, while the skin and hair uses rest on anecdote.

green-coffee-bean-extract.text: Users take green coffee bean extract as a fat-loss pill aimed at a leaner physique. It has been studied for blood pressure and metabolic markers, and its best-known weight-loss study was retracted, so the appearance claim is largely untested.

chain: Lower body fat, more muscle definition
chromium-picolinate.text: Chromium picolinate is marketed to curb sugar cravings, cut fat and support muscle development. Reviews have looked at body weight and lean mass and report no reliable effects, so the link to a leaner look is a marketing belief.

detox-slimming-teas.text: Users drink detox and slimming teas to de-bloat and drop scale weight quickly before events or photos. The change is typically fluid and gut contents rather than fat, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.

chain: Flatter-looking stomach for a short time
laxatives-for-weight-loss.text: Some people take laxatives to drop scale weight and look flatter. Reviews describe the loss as mostly water and classify the behaviour as purging linked to eating disorders, so it is documented as a weight-control practice rather than a fat-loss method.

chain: Lower body fat, leaner face and body
compounded-semaglutide-microdosing-glp-1.text: Users take compounded or gray-market semaglutide, often at below-label amounts, to cut appetite and body fat for a leaner face and physique. Fat loss is established at approved doses in trials, while the microdosing version has not been studied.

calorie-deficit-calorie-counting.text: A calorie deficit tracked by counting is the baseline method in looksmaxxing circles for cutting body fat to reveal jawline, cheekbones and abs. Fat loss from a deficit is well established, while evidence specific to facial appearance is limited.

high-protein-diet.text: Users eat protein-forward to hold onto muscle while dieting and to stay full on fewer calories, giving a leaner, more muscular look. The muscle and fullness benefits are supported in studies, while claims of better hair and skin are untested.

omad-one-meal-a-day.text: Users eat all daily food in one sitting as a simple way to run a calorie deficit and lean out. It is a form of time-restricted eating, and no trials have tested OMAD specifically for appearance.

extended-water-fasting.text: Forum users discuss 2 to 7 day water fasts for quick fat loss before a cut or lean bulk. Research on prolonged fasts shows early weight loss that includes water and lean tissue, and appearance outcomes are not studied.

5-2-diet-alternate-day-fasting.text: Users follow 5:2 or alternate-day fasting to build a weekly calorie deficit and lean out. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary dieting, and appearance outcomes themselves are not studied.

chain: Appetite drops and water is shed
keto-diet.text: Users adopt keto to lose fat and look leaner, and some also pursue it for skin and hormone benefits. Trials show short-term weight loss with little edge over other diets once calories are matched.

lion-diet.text: Followers of the lion diet eat only ruminant meat, salt and water as a stricter carnivore diet, citing leaner bodies and clearer skin. No trials exist on it, and the appearance benefits rest on anecdote.

chain: Alternate high and low carb days
carb-cycling-refeeds.text: Users alternate higher and lower carbohydrate days, with refeeds around training, to lean out while keeping gym performance. Direct evidence is thin, and fat loss in studies tracks total calories.

volume-eating.text: Users build meals around vegetables, fruit and other bulky low-calorie foods to stay full while cutting. Energy density is a studied factor in dieting, though volume eating itself has not been studied as a looksmaxxing method.

avoiding-ultra-processed-foods.text: Users cut ultra-processed foods to lose fat and, in some circles, to improve skin. UPF intake is linked to health outcomes in observational studies, and appearance trials of avoiding them have not been done.

cotton-ball-diet.text: The cotton ball diet is a fad in which people swallow cotton balls to feel full and eat less, aiming for a thinner look. It is untested in trials, and health experts have condemned it.

master-cleanse-juice-cleanse.text: Users do the Master Cleanse or juice cleanses for one to seven days to de-bloat and drop weight quickly. Medical sources report temporary weight loss and no evidence for the detox claims.

chain: Drier, more defined look for a day
dehydration-cuts-water-cutting.text: Borrowed from combat sports, water cutting is used by physique-focused users to look drier and more defined for photos or events. The look is visible within hours and fades on rehydration, and the practice is not studied as a looksmaxxing method.

zone-2-cardio.text: Users do conversational-pace cardio as a low-stress way to burn calories and support fat loss without cutting into training recovery. It is popular in fitness and longevity circles, and zone-specific research for appearance goals is limited.

hiit.text: HIIT is promoted as a time-efficient way to lose fat and build conditioning for a leaner physique. It is well supported for fitness, and trials show fat-loss effects modest and similar to steady cardio.

10k-steps-neat.text: Users raise daily steps and everyday activity (NEAT) as an easy way to widen a calorie deficit and lean out. The health benefits of walking are well supported, and fat-loss effects vary between people.

12-3-30-incline-walking.text: The viral 12% incline, 3 mph, 30 minute walk is used as a low-impact fat-loss routine for a leaner physique. Evidence is limited to one small exploratory study.

rucking.text: Users walk with a weighted backpack as low-impact cardio that burns more than plain walking and loads the back, legs and posture muscles. It is popular in fitness circles, and appearance-specific trials have not been done.

chain: More energy drawn from body fat
fasted-cardio.text: Fasted morning cardio is a staple of bodybuilding-style cutting, where practitioners believe low carbohydrate stores shift energy use toward body fat. Direct research on it is limited.

sauna-sweat-suits.text: Users sweat in saunas or sweat suits to drop water weight and look leaner for a day, and some believe the sweating burns fat. The weight change is visible on the scale and returns with rehydration, and direct fat-loss research is limited.

spot-reduction-exercises.text: Users do ab routines and face or jaw exercises to slim a specific area. Studies cited by reference works find that fat is lost across the body rather than locally, so the local-slimming idea remains a belief.

bulk-and-cut-body-recomposition.text: Borrowed from bodybuilding, users alternate calorie surplus and deficit phases, or attempt slow recomposition, to add muscle and then reveal it. The approach has little direct trial evidence in the sources reviewed.

macro-tracking-apps.text: Users log meals in apps such as MyFitnessPal to hit calorie and protein targets while cutting or bulking. Tracking is popular in physique circles, and self-reported intake carries accuracy limits.
